newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - Sept 1.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - Sept 1.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

An Australian Bureau of Statistics report, released yesterday, confirms what many have suspected - the financially rich are the information rich. The figures indicate more than half of all homes with incomes of over A$57,000 a year have personal computers Page 1.

According to the ANZ Bank's job series, which measures the number of vacancies advertised in major metropolitan newspapers, the labour market remains frail, with vacancies down 14.4 per cent over the past year, falling 2.3 per cent in seasonally adjusted erms in August. Page 2.

Renegade Senator Mal Colston, who as deputy president of the Senate was in the chair, used his vote last night to block an amendment supported by all other non-Government Senators and, in the process, saved industry between A$1 billion and A$2 billion. Colston voted with the Government on an amendment seeking to
lower the level at which noise insulation has to be provided for houses around airports. Page 4.

The New South Wales Court of Appeal's unanimous judgement in Vabu v the Commissioner of Taxation - the Crisis Couriers case - has cleared the way for courier companies and potentially many other firms to avoid paying superannuation, payroll tax, PAYE and employee leave entitlements by hiring workers as "independent contractors". Page 5.
THE AUSTRALIAN

As employers warned any delay or emasculation of the Federal Government's Workplace Relations Bill would be "unconscionable conduct", Australian Democrats Leader Cheryl Kernot said an agreement on the Bill was "a long way off" and vowed not to tolerate an watering down of the role of the Industrial Relations Commission. Page 1.

Senator Brian Harradine yesterday rejected the Senate Telstra committee's finding that the Government did not need to privatise part of Telstra to create the long-awaited National Heritage Fund, and he supported the Government's plan to use the
sale moneyto set up the A$1 billion environment fund. His decision significantly improves the Coalition's chances of selling one third of the national carrier. Page 1.

Opposition Leader Kim Beazley looks set to join Prime Minister John Howard in voting for a private member's Bill, introduced yesterday by Victorian backbencher Kevin Andrews, to overturn the Northern Territory's landmark voluntary euthanasia law. The Bill removes the right of Territory assemblies to make laws on mercy killings. Page 1.

Despite repeated questioning in the Senate, Communications Minister Richard Alston yesterday refused to say whether the Government would deliver its election promise for a full public inquiry into the cross media limits. The inquiry now seems unlikely as,until now, Alston has been promising to announce the chairperson and the terms of reference for the inquiry "in due course". Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

Despite a Senate inquiry declaring yesterday that the Federal Government's sale of one-third of Telstra should not proceed, the Coalition believes it can still win the crucial support of two Independent Senators, Mal Colston and Brian Harradine, who yesterday left open the option of supporting the partial sale. Page 1.

Despite Prime Minister John Howard's sudden decision to call an inquiry into health insurance and take personal control of the approvals process, Federal Health Minister Michael Wooldridge yesterday described the increases as "normal" and
claimed he knew bout the health insurance premium increases before the Budget. Page 1.

Police and private detectives are investigating the disappearance of the gold medal for the 200 metres freestyle won at the Seoul Olympics by former Australian swimming champion Duncan Armstrong, who has grave fears the medal has been stolen. Page 1.

Police believe they know the identity of the two men responsible for the bashing murder of Brian Hagland at Bondi early on Saturday following investigations centred on how the men fled and where they went. Hagland's girlfriend, Connie Casey, who witnessedthe murder, was yesterday helping police compile a computerised FACE image of the suspects. Page 3.
THE AGE

Although Victorian Health Minister Rob Knowles yesterday confirmed the Government would not go ahead with plans to move St Vincent's Hospital from Fitzroy to Knox, he warned other inner city hospitals that the Government was still determined to move health resources to the more populous outer suburbs. Page A1.

The Opposition parties expressed their support for the public ownership of Telstra in a report released yesterday which claimed the telecommunications giant would have to pay retrenched workers A$1.2 billion and an extra A$160 million for

its own part-priatisation. However, Government Senators said the proposed one-third sale of Telstra would boost the Budget by A$345 million a year and the economy by A$2.4 billion by 2002-03. Page A1.

A study on literacy by Melbourne University researchers reveals that one in five students is reading well below the reading standards expected by teachers and Federal Education Minister David Kemp says the Government would consider introducing national lieracy standards for grade 1 students in response to parents' complaints about poor reading standards.
Page A1.

Despite receiving support from Prime Minister John Howard and the Catholic Church, Liberal MP Kevin Andrews' anti-euthanasia bill introduced to Federal Parliament yesterday was condemned by Northern Territory Member Nick Dondas and South Australian MP Chrstine Gallus. Dondas criticised the bill for attempting to undermine the Territory's right to make its own laws and Gallus said the bill strives to reassert the power of doctors over patients. Page A3.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
